To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relation of obesity and physical activity to physical self-perception is moderated by cardiovascular fitness.

(1) physical activity and fitness were positively associated with self-perceptions of physical appearance, sport competence, and global physical self-concept in rural elementary school children; (2) the relation between physical activity and self-perceptions of appearance, sport competence and global physical self-perception was stronger in girls than in boys; and (3) cardiovascular fitness moderated the relation between estimates of obesity, as measured by BMI, and self-perceptions in girls but not in boys.
the relation between obesity and physical self-worth was moderated by cardiovascular fitness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relations between physical self-perceptions and estimates of obesity, and the possible moderating effect of cardiovascular fitness.
the relations among physical self-perceptions, estimates of body fat, and physical fitness in rural elementary school boys and girls.
the effects of obesity on children's physical and social self-perceptions, and how these effects are moderated by physical activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between obesity and self-esteem is not as simple as it may seem, and that there are many factors to consider.
the use of a single measure of obesity (BMI) is not a reliable measure of obesity and should not be used as the sole indicator for the presence of obesity in children.
the relationship between obesity and self-esteem is complex and multifaceted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for estimating the number of calories burned during a workout.
we are interested in how children's physical fitness relates to their physical self-perceptions and their perceptions of their body weight.
the relationship between obesity and physical self-concept is mediated by cardiovascular fitness in children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use our understanding of the brain's reward systems to help people lose weight and improve their physical health.
we need more studies to understand how the brain responds to different types of exercise, including resistance training, in people who are overweight or obese.
there are many ways to improve physical activity in children and adolescents and that there is no "one size fits all" approach to increasing physical activity in youth.
